title: Docker Compose for Multi-Container Apps
description: Run multi-container applications using Docker Compose and a single docker-compose.yml file.

data.text: **Docker Compose** is a tool for defining and running multi-container Docker applications. Instead of running several `docker run` commands, you describe all your services, networks, and volumes in a single `docker-compose.yml` file and let Compose handle the lifecycle.
A `docker-compose.yml` file is declarative — you describe the desired state (which containers you want, how they connect, and what configuration they need), and Compose figures out how to achieve it.

data.title: A simple two-service stack
data.content: This compose file defines a web application backed by a PostgreSQL database. Compose automatically creates a network and handles DNS between services.
data.code:
services:
  web:
    build: ./.
    ports:
      - "3000:3000"
    depends_on:
      - db
    environment:
      DATABASE_URL: postgres://postgres:secret@db:5432/mydb

  db:
    image: postgres:16-alpine
    environment:
      POSTGRES_DB: mydb
      POSTGRES_USER: postgres
      POSTGRES_PASSWORD: secret
    volumes:
      - db-data:/var/lib/postgresql/data

volumes:
  db-data:

data.title: Starting and stopping a stack
data.content: Bring the stack up in the background, check status, interact with a service, and tear it down.
data.code:
docker compose up -d
docker compose ps
docker compose exec web sh
docker compose logs -f web
docker compose stop
docker compose down -v

data.title: Compose v1 vs v2
data.text: The older syntax was `docker-compose` (hyphenated). Modern Docker uses the `docker compose` plugin (no hyphen). If you have an older installation, you may need to use `docker-compose` instead.

The `depends_on` key controls the order in which services start. However, it only waits for the container to be *running* — not for the application inside to be *ready*. For production readiness, you should use health checks.

data.title: Health check in Compose
data.content: A health check tells Docker to periodically test the service before considering it ready.
data.code:
services:
  web:
    build: .
    ports:
      - "3000:3000"
    depends_on:
      db:
        condition: service_healthy

  db:
    image: postgres:16-alpine
    healthcheck:
      test: ["CMD-SHELL", "pg_isready -U postgres"]
      interval: 10s
      timeout: 5s
      retries: 5

data.text: By default, Compose places all services on a single network and sets up DNS so services can reach each other by their service name. Named volumes (declared under the top-level `volumes:` key) ensure that data survives container restarts.

data.caption: Docker Compose creates an isolated network and lets services discover each other by name.

data.title: Run a WordPress + MySQL stack
data.description: Practice Compose with a real multi-container application.
steps: Create a `docker-compose.yml` with wordpress and mysql services.
Map WordPress to port 8080 on the host.
Set the MySQL root password via an environment variable.
Open http://localhost:8080 in a browser and verify WordPress loads.
Run `docker compose down -v` to clean up.
data.expectedOutcome: WordPress is accessible in the browser and the MySQL data is stored in a named volume.

data.title: Key Takeaways
points: Docker Compose manages multi-container applications with a single YAML file.
Services can reference each other by name — Compose handles DNS automatically.
Use `depends_on` with health checks for proper startup ordering.
Named volumes keep data persistent across container restarts and `docker compose down`.
data.takeaway: Compose is the quickest way to run a full stack of dependent services for local development.
